title: Eye-Level Is Buy-Level
editorialNotes: Tier 1: brief says no product name; the renderer paints the fond wordmark on every cta-card, so Adi should confirm that is acceptable.

The "20-40% less" and "roughly 30% more" figures and the $100 to $115-$120 cart are the brief's own illustrative estimates with no citation; rendered inside body copy and a diagram, never as hero type. The cart example is hypothetical (10 items at 30%).

thread.element: price tag climbing a five-tier shelf rack to eye level
thread.startState: tag on the bottom shelf at a low price

copy.headline: The shelf in front of you is a paid advertisement. The cheapest version of what you want is usually by your feet.
Eye level is the most expensive real estate in the store.
items: Brands pay slotting fees to put their priciest products exactly where your gaze lands.
You're not choosing it. It was placed there.

copy.headline: Look down. Look up.
items: The bottom and top shelves are where the cheaper brands and bigger-value sizes get exiled.

copy.headline: Now look at the kids' cereal.
copy.body: Sugary brands sit at a child's eye level - about 3 feet up. That's not an accident either. The whole store is mapped to a sightline.

copy.headline: The math on one trip:
copy.body: If eye-level placement nudges you to the pricier pick on just 10 items, at roughly 30% more each, a $100 cart quietly becomes a $115-$120 cart. Every week.

copy.headline: The counter-move costs nothing:
items: Scan the whole shelf - top to bottom - before you grab.
Check the unit price, not the shelf price.
The deal is almost never at eye level.

copy.headline: The store is designed around where you look. Spending less starts with looking somewhere else.
